title: DARK MANSIONS: AI, Innovation, and Fermat’s Last Theorem
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video available here . Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work. We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration. Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. The paper concludes with reflections on the architectural changes that may be needed for the innovation that comes from what Andrew Wiles vividly describes as stumbling around in “dark mansions.” Bio: Joshua Cohen is a political philosopher. He has written on issues of democratic theory, freedom of expression, religious freedom, political equality, democracy and digital technology, good jobs, and global justice. His books include On Democracy (with Joel Rogers); Democracy and Associations ( with Joel Rogers); Philosophy, Politics, Democracy ; Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals ; and The Arc of the Moral Universe and Other Essays . He is co-editor of the Norton Introduction to Philosophy , now in its third edition. Cohen taught at MIT (1977-2005), Stanford (2005-2014), is currently on the faculty at Apple University, and is Distinguished Senior Fellow in Law, Philosophy, and Political Science at University of California, Berkeley. Cohen held the Romanell-Phi Beta Kappa Professorship in 2002-3; gave the Tanner Lectures at UC Berkeley in 2007; the Comte Lectures at LSE in 2012; and the Annual Lecture on Ethics and AI at Oxford in 2024. He is co-editor-in-chief of Boston Review . Sponsorship of an event does not constitute institutional endorsement of external speakers or views presented. location.name: Frist Health Center - A78B McLain Pavilion

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Join us for the official launch of Princeton’s Data and Intelligent Systems (DaIS), an initiative dedicated to supporting and expanding AI, Data Science, and Statistics research and education across the university. This event will introduce the DaIS vision and host a collaborative faculty symposium designed to foster interdisciplinary research partnerships. Event Details Date: September 30, 2026 Location: Frist Health Center - A78B McLain Pavilion The Launch: Introducing DaIS The event begins with a university-wide introduction to DaIS. This session will feature: Provost Jen Rexford to provide opening remarks. Tom Griffiths, Director of DaIS, will share insights on Princeton AI. Arthur Spirling, Director of DaIS, will share insights on Princeton Statistics and Data Science, and the education efforts of DaIS Faculty Research Collaboration Symposium Following the introductory remarks, the Faculty Research Collaboration Symposium will commence. This portion of the event is specifically for faculty members to present their research ideas and seek guidance and feedback from across disciplines on how AI and data science can support their work. The aim is to help create new productive collaborations among colleagues across the university. In addition, faculty previously in receipt of DaIS seed grants will present work that flowed from those efforts. Reception The conclusion of the event invites all to a light reception to mingle and connect with peers.

title: Statistically-Grounded Methods for Meaningful LLM Evaluation
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract: In cognitive science, the well-established task of statistical learning, i.e., picking up hidden regularities in sequences, has been linked to neural plasticity in humans. However, we found that LLMs are able to learn a hidden automaton structure entirely in context, simply by feeding them valid sequences from the automaton, and they learn it even faster when the structure reappears with new vocabulary. Building on this, I present Agentic Automata Learning, a framework to formalize what agents can infer from an environment. The agent's task is to identify a hidden automaton by querying an oracle. The framework generates instances of controllable difficulty and tests planning, hypothesis formation and memory, with formal efficiency metrics. We find that frontier models struggle as automata grow, their queries become less informative over time, and they fail at both planning and reasoning from evidence. Providing the agent with stateful scaffolding helps but doesn't close the gap. These results point to inferring structure from interaction as a key open challenge for building agents that can operate in unfamiliar environments. Bio: Gili Lior is a Ph.D. candidate in Natural Language Processing at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, advised by Prof. Gabriel Stanovsky. Her work has dealt with cognitively-motivated analysis and comparison between humans and LLMs, and her current research focuses on human-motivated LLM evaluations, leveraging statistical models to ensure that metrics reflect what users actually care about. She is also a research intern at Google Research working on evaluations of long horizon agentic tasks, and has previously interned at IBM Research and the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2). She is a recipient of the Council for Higher Education's fellowship program for excellent female Ph.D. students in hi-tech fields. Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

title: Securing LLMs Against Prompt Injection for Agentic Applications
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract : Prompt injection is widely recognized as a major security threat to AI agents, in which external untrusted data (websites, documents, and emails) may contain an injected prompt (“Ignore previous instructions and …”) that arbitrarily manipulates an agent’s operations. The best-defended existing LLMs still suffer from near-100% attack success rates (ASRs) under adaptive prompt-injection attacks. In this talk, I will discuss our latest efforts, SecPO and SecOPD, to fine-tune LLMs with an order-of-magnitude lower ASRs (0% -- 13.3%) against the current strongest prompt-injection attacks. Specifically, we (1) separate the trusted prompt and untrusted data into two input channels; (2) simulate strong adaptively attacked training samples for the model to learn robustness from; and (3) design the loss according to a principle that approximates a (nonexistent) secure-and-powerful LLM. Without a noticeable utility drop, our defended Qwen3.6-27B achieves security that generalizes to realistic agentic tasks with multiple trusted and untrusted messages. We fully open our training set with optimized injections, code for our recipe, and the defended model, which is more robust than industry-scale adversarially-trained GPT-5.5 in agentic tasks. Bio : Sizhe Chen is a Computer Science Ph.D. candidate at UC Berkeley’s Berkeley AI Research (BAIR), working with Prof. David Wagner. He studies real-world AI security problems with general and principled solutions. He developed StruQ, Meta-SecAlign, SecPO, and SecOPD, the most robust open LLMs against adaptive prompt injection attacks. His research has been supported by selective industry fundings, including NVIDIA Fellowship, Meta-BAIR Commons, and Google-BAIR Commons. Previously, he obtained an M.Eng. and a B.Eng. from Shanghai Jiao Tong University. https://sizhe-chen.github.io Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series
